utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Please be seated. May I ask Madam Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-94-2-S, the Prosecutor versus Dragan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And may we have the appearances, please, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours, I appear for the Prosecution. I'm Upawansa Yapa, with Ms. Patricia Sellers and Mr. Bill Smith. Ms. Diane Boles is our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning, to the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Howard Morrison and Tanja Radosavljevic for the accused Dragan Nikolic. I do understand that he is not receiving the commentary and translation at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So then we have to wait a second until it's functioning. May I ask you, Mr. Nikolic, can you now follow the proceedings in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There was no microphone for the accused when he answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Now the microphone is switched on. I ask you, can you follow the proceedings in a language you understand? No? So could you please exchange the microphone. May I try a third time. Can you now hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then let me take immediately the opportunity to ask you if you have any health problems today. Everything is fine with you, in this regard?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no problems at present. I had some minor complaints in the previous days, but they do not affect my ability to follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I just take the opportunity for some clarification. On Friday, the Prosecution filed a submission of a further amendment of the third amended indictment. This incorporates that what was discussed during the last hearing on the plea agreement, especially in paragraph 2. It says that Counts 1, persecutions; count 2, murder; count 4, torture; that you are charged for having committed these crimes; whereas, count 3, it's limited to aiding and abetting. And in addition to this, in paragraph 36, it reads now "widespread and systematic attack" instead of "or systematic attack." I think - please object if you think otherwise. It's not necessary to repeat the entire plea procedure because it's just the same we discussed the last time. You understand that it is charged that the crimes you admitted have been committed in the framework of a widespread and systematic attack directed against the civilian population; is that correct, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask the Defence, any objections that from now on this further amendment of the third amended indictment forms part of the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then for the purpose of clarification, this indictment forms now the only basis for the now-following hearing. The mere purpose of this hearing is to receive, pursuant to Rule 100, information that may assist the Trial Chamber in determining an appropriate sentence. This means completing the picture, mitigating factors, aggravating factors as we all know of it from the settled jurisprudence of this Tribunal. However, it might be that the testimony might be -- go beyond this indictment. In this case, the Trial Chamber does not want to intervene. This does, however, not mean that the factual basis of the plea agreement can or will be broadened or limited. In case a witness should testify beyond the scope of the indictment, it's not necessary to object respect vis-a-vis especially a victim, as it is the special mandate of this Tribunal also to assist in reconciliation and finding the truth and this may forbid and it goes without saying that it's the respect, vis-a-vis the victim, not to intervene. Today it is announced that we will hear three witnesses. May I ask beforehand that we can clarify this immediately for the purpose -- also of our technicians. The first witness will testify without any protective measures; the second one under pseudonym and image distortion; the third one under pseudonym, image, and voice distortion and private session. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: If I may inform Your Honours. In respect to have third witness, it will be pseudonym, image, and voice distortion, but not private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Then this has been changed; we can delete it. Thank you for this clarification. And last week and under the submission in the sentencing brief annex it was planned to hear Ms. Maria Zepter, an expert. Now we have in front of us dated the 31st of October this statement under Rule 94 bis (C). May I ask the Defence, are you in agreement with this envisaged procedure?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. The Defence is confident that if in any statement, expert or otherwise, there is a opinion stated which goes so far beyond the scope of the indictment that it would be improper to take it into consideration, that that is a matter that can properly be left to the discretion of the Judges, and I am confident it will be so dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Coming back to the statement under Rule 94 bis of Maria Zepter. You've got this document? Was it filed last week? And the question would be: Pursuant to Rule 94 bis (B)(i), do you accept the expert witness statement without request for the foreseen time limit and without the necessity to testify in person?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. The only caveat that the Defence would always have in those circumstances is it may be necessary to comment on the statement in conclusion, specifically to identify those areas where the Defence would say it goes beyond or may go beyond the scope of the indictment. But as to the generality of the statement, it seems, with great respect, to the Trial Chamber's view of her expertise, that most of it falls into the category of what one might call common sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. So I take it that you accept it, and no doubt it has to be discussed if you so want. Finally, we had Annex B to the sentencing brief of the OTP, that we can clarify also these matters; there were three statements included. May I ask: Is it the intention of the Prosecution still to tender these three statements under Rule 92 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: It is, Your Honours. I have had discussions with my learned friends on the opposite side in respect of these statements. The position is that we will be moving to have only the statements of two of those witnesses, that is, number 1 and 2. Attached to those statements were some of the statements that had been taken during the time of the investigations. Those will not be tendered. It will be only the impact statements, not the others. So that is in respect of those two witnesses, the first two witnesses. If Your Honours would please, to see Annex B, the witnesses are -

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: SU-115 and SU-230.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So in other words you withdraw SU-025.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As regards the two first one, your intention is to tender all the statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Not all the statements but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But could you specify.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would have been -- I would have clarified this position in my present opening remarks, but I can straight away inform Your Honours that the statements that we will tender for admission would be in respect of SU-115, the statement made on the 8th of October, 2003. And in respect of Witness SU-230, the statement made on the 9th of October, 2003. Those two statements only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- They are withdrawn -- just to repeat because my microphone was not switched on, unfortunately -- the other parts of SU-115 and SU-230 are withdrawn. For the remaining two statements of 8 October and 9 October respectively, may I ask the Defence, as it is a matter on the acts on conduct of the accused, does the Defence waive the right of cross-examination and accept the mere statements as they are before us?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, this is a matter which I discussed with my learned friend last Friday. It seems to the Defence that if it's limited to those matters which my learned friend has now indicated, there would be neither profit nor sense in calling for those witnesses to be called and unnecessarily distressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then the scope of today's hearing is clarified. We know about tomorrow. On Wednesday we will hear the professor from the Max Planck Institute in Freiberg and on Thursday we'll start with the expert, Dr. Grosselfinger. May I ask the parties to be prepared if time so allows to start and hopefully even to conclude the final submissions on Thursday. Let's give it a try. But it's premature finally to decide on this. Let's now go medias in res, and may I ask the Prosecution to start. The floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours. The proceedings in this case have reached the stage at which Your Honours must determine the appropriate sentence that should be imposed on the accused. This case has certain special features. It is not a case that has gone to trial; the accused has pleaded guilty to the indictment in its entirety; the Prosecution and the Defence have entered into a plea agreement. The Statute of the Tribunal makes provision for the punishment of offenders and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, in accordance with the Statute, provide for certain guidelines for the purpose of sentencing. Your Honours have decided to call two -- call for two reports, one dealing with the range of sentences for the crimes in the indictment in the former Yugoslavia, in the states of the Council of Europe and other major legal systems. It was also ordered that a report be furnished on the sentencing practice developed in the states on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, international courts and other courts. The second report as named by Your Honours was to do with the accused's socialisation. The Prosecution in this instance is performing a duty of assisting Your Honours by placing before you certain relevant material and also by making submissions on the matter of sentencing. The duty cast on the Defence as respected by my learned friends will not be any different. We are not aiming to present a case any graver than or different from what has been admitted to by the accused. In fact, it could be said that there is no contest between the Prosecution and the Defence on the central issue in the proceedings that commences today. What I propose to do now is to indicate to Your Honours very briefly the agenda of the Prosecution presentation today. I think that it is the right moment to clarify certain matters in the Prosecution sentencing brief. The Prosecution -- this has been already inverted to in answer to your questions, in answer to Your Honours's questions, but I will repeat my answers. The Prosecution is not calling the psychologist to testify on the psychological impact on the victims and the witnesses. Instead, we have filed a statement of Dr. Zepter under Rule 94 bis. In respect of the statements we have filed, I wish to inform Your Honours that we would seek to admit only two of those statements; the statements I refer to are in Annex B of the Prosecution brief and are of issue 115 and issue 230. We wish to withdraw the statement of issue 025. There's a further qualification, if I may: Especially the two statements are dated 8 October 2003 and 9 October 2003. Documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In order to save time, the Trial Chamber convened briefly. Those documents you tendered and as there were no objections by the Defence, are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Documents in Annex D will not be made use of. That's another information that I wish to present to Your Honour. We propose to call three witnesses today. They will not be providing any additional information as such but will confirm the salient features of the case that have been admitted by the accused. Some significant photo stills will be introduced, which I feel confident will give Your Honours a better and a clearer understanding of the circumstances of the case. I informed Your Honours that there will be three witnesses. The first witness will be led by my learned friend here, Mr. William Smith. The second witness will be led by me. And the third witness will be led by Ms. Patricia Sellers. May I now ask my learned friend, Mr. William Smith, to lead the first witness. I thank Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I'm informed that my learned friend will do a short presentation in respect of the evidence to be tendered by the first witness. I thank Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, my learned friends. Your Honours, just to further continue with what Mr. Yapa has said this morning, there will be presentations today, as discussed last Friday, in relation to the widespread and systematic nature of the attack that surrounded Susica camp and how Susica camp fitted in the context of that attack, as well as some presentations in relation to the sexual violence count and also a short presentation in relation to the murder count. The first presentation hopes to put Susica camp and the role that the accused played in it into a context which will help Your Honours judge this case accordingly. This presentation, Your Honour, will take about 25 minutes. The third purpose of this presentation is to provide some visual aids to assist in the understanding of the testimony that will come today. For example, the first witness has poor vision, and she is unable to see any photos or videos, and hopefully this presentation will put her evidence and the other witnesses' evidence into some context. If I ask Your Honours to place your computer monitors into computer evidence mode as there'll be some visual photographs and maps that will be seen on the screen as -- as this presentation or submission continues. And at the end of this submission, Your Honours, there'll be a five-minute video of Susica camp to help further understanding the witness's testimony and the indictment even further. The accused has already admitted to the crimes he committed at Susica, that they related to a widespread and systematic attack directed at the civilian population, specifically the Muslim and non-Serb community. He also admitted that from May 1992 until September 1992 all those Muslims and other non-Serbs that did not flee to other areas before the takeover of the town, they were forcibly transferred from the municipality, leaving virtually no Muslim or non-Serb in the Vlasenica area. How did this attack happen and what was the function of Susica camp in the ethnic cleansing of Vlasenica? A look at the geography, ethnic mix, and political policies of the area in 1992, with a brief chronology of events, will provide the answers. Vlasenica municipality was located in Eastern Bosnia about 30 kilometres west of the Serbian border. Before the takeover of Vlasenica in 1992 by Bosnian Serb forces, about 34.000 people lived there, belonging to two ethnic groups, Muslims and Serbs. Slightly over half the population was Muslim and slightly under half was of Serb ethnicity. The political and administrative centre of the municipality is the town of Vlasenica. 7.500 citizens lived in the town, of whom two-thirds were Muslim and one-third Serb. Notably, in other towns and villages almost all had an absolute majority of one ethnic group over another. Each village, therefore, had an ethnic identity. These identities became a source of tension in the early 1990s as ethnic and national sentiment--

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please read more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I will slow down. I apologise to the people in the booth. With the disintegration of the former Yugoslavia, political loyalties became divided along ethnic lines. In tandem to the political divisions, military separation commenced and movements for independence developed along ethnic lines. Bosnian Serbs of Vlasenica formed irregular paramilitary units in Milici and Misari. At this time, elements of the JNA became aligned with the national Serbian cause and in mid-1991 the Muslim refusal to join the mass mobilisation for the outbreak of hostilities in Croatia helped to consolidate the Serb dominance of the JNA. Ethnic tension further increased in Vlasenica in late 1991 with the political developments at a country-wide level. By the 21st of November, 1991, Bosnian Serb leaders had declared the formation of the Serb autonomous regions. Vlasenica was included in the Romanija-Birac region along with other neighbouring municipalities. Outside of strict military formations, some Serb citizens of Vlasenica were being secretly armed by Serbian leaders. This weapons distribution intensified and became more open in early 1992. Some Muslims distributed weapons as well, but not enough to resist the Serb forces in the takeover to come. Exactly five months after the declaration of the Serb regions, Serb forces, including local Serb units and a Serb-dominated JNA corps swiftly took over the town of Vlasenica on the 21st of April, 1992. These forces encountered virtually no Muslim resistance. JNA tanks were stationed around the city and blocked the streets; the largest hotel in town, the Hotel Panorama, was taken over by the army as well as other key government, social, and commercial buildings. Muslims were ordered to surrender weapons they had to the JNA and local Serbs. They generally complied. On the day of the takeover, a new Serb municipal government was imposed. Parliament was disbanded and the already-formed Serb crisis staff took over the power in the municipality. The Serb authorities took control of the police and its station, the court and its building, and other civic institutions. Serb individuals were placed into leading political positions, which in some cases, like the chief of police and president of court, were formerly held by Muslims. Only days after the takeover, Serbian men who were not otherwise involved in military activity like the accused were mobilised and placed into either army or police units. Some 20 days later, about mid-May, with the Serb takeover of the town successfully achieved, the JNA left Vlasenica, leaving behind its equipment, vehicles, and ammunition for local Serb forces to use. Following the takeover and at a greater pace as time passed, the policy of the new Serb authorities designed to remove Muslims and non-Serbs from the municipality became manifest. The practical implementation of this policy broadly occurred in three phases, namely the disarmament and restriction of Muslim civilians; the arrest, interrogation, and detention of Muslims; and attacks on Muslim villages within the municipality. Neither activity happened independently of the other but occurred as three linked operations designed to expel Muslims and non-Serbs from the municipality. It's not the purpose nor the scope of this submission to detail the destruction, the beatings, the killings, and the sexual assaults that accompanied the ethnic cleansing of Muslims in the town and surrounding villages in Vlasenica from April to September 1992, but suffice to say that the human cost was severe. During the initial four-week period after the takeover, military-age men were usually the target of intimidation and harassment by Serb forces, whether police or army. Muslim men were taken for interrogation at the police station and detained there, or alternatively, transferred to the courthouse jail around the corner. Both the police and court cells were jam-packed with Muslim men. Many were brutally beaten. Most of these men, if not released beforehand, were later transferred to Susica camp when it opened in early June 1992. Although this process of targeting Muslim males for arrest, interrogation, detentions, and beatings occurred before the main attacks on the villages surrounding the town, it continued in parallel with the attacks and in conjunction with the operation of the main Vlasenica detention facility, Susica camp, until its closure in late September or early October 1992. The attacks on Muslim towns and villages were unlawful. These villages were full of women, children, elderly, as well as men of military age. These attacks began in May 1992, and -- at the latest and continued until September 1992, when Muslim civilians from a vast area of Vlasenica had been completely expelled and transferred to other places. In this process, significant numbers of Muslim civilians were killed and their houses destroyed. Only isolated and minimal resistance was met during these assaults.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, please be asked to read slower. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: -- Were done in an organised way. Typically, Serb forces physically entered the villages after prolonged shelling and then looted and burned houses. Serb forces captured, killed, and otherwise maltreated Muslim residents. They also searched surrounding forests for Muslims who were in the process of escaping. These attacks were carried out by hundreds of Serb men from the army and the police. If not killed or injured in these attacks, residents either fled east, towards Cerska, a Muslim-controlled village in Vlasenica, or west towards Kladanj, attempting to leave the municipality with whatever means they had available. Or they were placed on the buses at the bus station in the centre of town and transferred to another municipality. Or they were captured and taken to Susica camp. Some of the most violent attacks occurred in mid-May, with the most brutal one being in the village of Zakoplaca, where 16 Muslim civilians were murdered. On the map, you can see the attacked village by the red shading. Another round of attacks occurred in radio late May in the village of Gradina and the surrounding area. As you can see from the map, Gradina as well as Zacoplaca was on the main road route to Serb-dominated areas such as Valici in the east of the municipality. Further and more far-reaching attacks against Muslim villages occurred in as late as June 1992. The biggest concentration of the Muslim population was in the process of being removed from Vlasenica. The village attacks continued further north into the municipality through to August 1992, resulting in the destruction of Muslim homes and tremendous grief for entire families. At this time, a line of defence was finally formed between the Serb forces and the newly-formed Muslim resistance. However, the majority of the Muslim population from these villages had already been driven out. In the town of Vlasenica, whilst these village attacks were occurring, the Muslim residents were being targeted. Unlike the villages, there was less destruction of Muslim property in the town, with the exception of looting that occurred after residents were arrested or had fled their homes. However, the harassment and general persecution of Muslims in the town was intense. After the initial period of targeting Muslim men specifically by June 1992, no age or gender was spared from persecution. Families were arrested and taken to Susica camp to wait for orders to be transferred to other municipalities. Houses were searched, vacated homes looted and occupied by Serb forces carrying out the ethnic cleansing. Those not detained had their movement restricted and many were forced to sign loyalty oaths. By the end of July, the Muslim workforce was severely diminished. The only Muslims that were working were doing so by force, whilst they were being detained at Susica camp. Large numbers of Muslims from other nearby municipalities, such as Sekovici and Rogatica were also brought to Vlasenica and detained first at the high school, in the case of the men from Sekovici, and then at Susica camp. Not only was the camp being used as a focal transit point for the removal of Muslims in the municipality, but it was also used as a detention facility for others. Those not detained at Susica and then transferred were forced to leave from the bus station or other places on buses provided by the newly-formed Serb authorities. Many Muslim civilians did leave this way, but military-age men were often arrested, detained, and taken to Susica while attempting to do so. Around August 1992, the mosque in the town of Vlasenica shared the same fate as other Muslim buildings in many villages; that is to say it was destroyed. In late September 1992, there were virtually no Muslims left in the municipality, other than Muslim detainees at Susica camp numbering over a hundred men. The context in which the accused committed his crimes is made clear by considering that Muslim civilians were completely expelled from Vlasenica. Their homes were destroyed, and over 700 Muslim civilians were killed and/or are still missing and who are presumed dead. Of those, approximately 200 were last seen alive at Susica camp. The accused was well aware that his crimes were part of this broader attack against the civilian population because he participated in the attacks on numerous villages before he accepted his position of command at Susica camp. The Prosecution are saying that the accused is not the sole commander of the camp but he had some command responsibility there. The very nature of Susica camp itself makes this connection apparent. The camp played a central role in the ethnic cleansing of Vlasenica, as mentioned earlier, its use as a transit facility facilitated the removal of Muslim civilians from the municipality. It was run by the police and the army, whose headquarters were only 2 kilometres away. Despite the closeness to those ultimately responsible for the camp, it was well hidden in a valley at the edge of town. As a commander of Susica camp, the accused played a significant role in the forced transfer of detainees displaced from their lawful places of residence and expelled to other parts of Bosnia. The Prosecution accepts that the accused was not the orchestrator nor the planner of this policy but submits that he was significant and active contributor to its implementation. The camp itself, an old army training ground consisted or two warehouses, Muslim civilians being held in the large empty one, often referred by witnesses as the hangar, which you can see on the left-hand side of the photo. The accused and the camp guards used a small white house separated from the hangar by about 15 metres, which you can see in the front of the hangar in the photo. These -- these buildings were in a small compound which formed a yard which was fenced. This photo depicts a side view of the hangar where Muslim civilians were detained. The camp operated for four months, from June to the end of September 1992. The length of time Muslims were kept varied from a few hours to several months. Over the four-month period, between 2.000 and 8.000 non-Serb civilians were detained at the camp. Those that were detained were almost exclusively Muslim. At any one time, over 500 people were imprisoned in that hangar, although the numbers in the camp fluctuated. The accused was present almost every day once he started his duties there in early June. He can be seen in this photo patrolling the perimeter fence on the 2nd of September, 2000, one month before the camp closed, when the first and only international monitoring delegation visited it. The accused and other guards controlled detainee movements by keeping them in the hangar for almost the entire 24 hours of the day. The guardhouse, with window views onto the front entrance of the hangar, was well placed to ensure that the accused and other guards stopped any detainees from escaping. Most if not all of the detainees, were civilian, which included at times large numbers of women, babies, young children, and the elderly. Sick, injured, and handicapped people were also detained at the camp. Few, if any, male detainees were active members of any armed resistance to the Serb attacks, nor were they captured in their involvement in armed conflict. There was no lawful reason for the detention; they weren't alleged criminals, threats to state security, nor was their own security under threat. Ove Bring, an international representative from the conference for security and cooperation in Europe, who was on the Monitoring Mission to the camp on the 2nd of September, 1992 reported, "Susica was a unique facility among the detention sites that we visited. It was just an empty shed that people were put into. There was no structure for receiving internees and the arbitrariness seemed overwhelming." As a commander at the camp, the accused played an important role in these detentions. He, with others, was responsible for detainees' confinement and security of the compound. The conditions at the camp were appalling. Usually the number of detainees was between 300 to 500; however, it fluctuated as people were arrived and were transferred out. At 35 metres long and 13 metres wide, the detainees were packed tight against each other. If 400 people were detained at the camp at one time, each detainee would have had about square metre to sit in. Sleeping facilities were inadequate. Detainees slept on the concrete floor of the hangar with little or no bedding. Apart from blankets, former JNA uniforms were given to some women and children. The floor was usually wet or damp, often there was not enough space to lie down or stretch out. At times detainees often slept sitting up, leaning against fellow detainees.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, just a little more slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'll slow down, Your Honour. On several occasions the accused took bedding such as blankets from a detainee then beat or mistreated people who had given these men blankets. Detainees exhibited constant exhaustion. Food was both of little quantity and poor quality. It was distributed only once per day and was often spoiled and did not meet basic nutritional needs. Detainees were constantly hungry, becoming emaciated and often sick. Muslims outside the camp tried to bring detainees food, but the Serb guards often took these supplies for their own consumption. Food and water was often withheld and seen as a form of punishment for the detainees, especially for those detainees who were constantly beaten. The CSCE delegation, visiting on the 2nd of September, noted in their report, "Detainees appear to be haggard, pale, and thin. There can be little doubt that most are hungry." The heat, poor ventilation, and hygienic conditions, lack of opportunity to shower, or use toilet facilities or change clothes produced an overpowering and rancid odour in the cramped hangar. Detainees were allowed to go to the toilet outside the hangar at one or two scheduled times in the day. If a detainee needed to relieve him or herself at times, they had to use a bucket -- at other times they had to use a bucket as a toilet in the open hangar with no privacy. No medical care was provided to sick detainees, they were not separated, and were forced to remain in the hangar in close contact with others. Detainees were becoming ill because of lack of good food and hygiene facilities. They suffered from severe toothaches, head lice, and fell sick from illnesses such as dysentery. The accused, in his role as commander, provided no medical care or medicine to those who suffered from illness or to those who were constantly beaten. For those well enough, many were forced to work picking vegetables in the field from the camp, harvesting crops, providing other skills or unskilled labour. Others were ordered to bury other Muslim civilians who did not survive in the village attacks. These inhumane conditions at the camp made it almost impossible for detainees to cope with the active mistreatment that the accused, other guards, and other soldiers directed towards them, their families, and their friends. At the camp the accused brutally mistreated male detainees, causing at least nine of them to die. Some men were beaten inside the hangar at an area known as the punishment corner, and others were assaulted outside at the A-pole, which can be seen in the photo. This second photo shows the detainees' view of the A-pole from inside the hangar. Many of those that didn't survive the beatings were left to die in the punishment corner, which was inside the hangar. They were in the full view of other detainees. Some men disappeared after beatings. Often the accused deprived beaten detainees of food and water. At the camp, many of the detained women were subjected to sexual assault, including rape. Camp guards and other men entered the camp and took women out of the hangar night where they were raped and sexual assaulted at other locations. Detainees were told to remain silent in the hangar and feared being singled out and abused if they made a noise. On other occasions, detainees were terrorised by the accused when he cocked his pistol and thrust it into a detainee's mouth and pulled the trigger of an unloaded weapon. The accused also subjected detainees to cruel and arbitrary punishments, such as ordering one detainee to sit in water for a length of time. Similarly, the accused refused detainees to go to the toilet on some occasions. The accused also humiliated and verbally abused detainees with insulting terms, such as "balija" or other references to their Muslim religion or ethnicity. These acts were committed within the sight and earshot of fellow prisoners. The cumulative mistreatment, especially horrified and anguished detainees, because it was meted out to their family members, their friends, and their acquaintances. This criminal conduct committed by the accused, guards, and other soldiers created an atmosphere of terror at the camp. Detainees wondered whether they or a family member would be the next victim. Mothers hushed their children, while women hid their faces and attempted to look older and uglier for fearing to be selected as the next rape victim. Detainees kept silent and lowered their heads and eyes, dreading that they would draw attention to themselves and be abused. This fear agonised detainees throughout their detention at Susica camp. Ove Bring reports from his visit on the 2nd of September, 1992. "The atmosphere within the main building was extremely tense and overbearing. It was also very quiet. No one of the detainees said anything. It was obvious that the detainees were very scared and they dared not speak with us and they avoided us. The fact that the detainees at Susica appeared very scared and subdued gave me an eerie feeling." The accused contributed to this atmosphere of terror substantially. Not solely by his own direct physical acts on the detainees but because of his significant influence as a commander at the camp over the detainees, the way that they were treated. The accused told detainees that is he had absolute control over them and that they were at his mercy. He told them that he was their God and that in the camp he was the God, the stick, and the law. He was constantly heavily armed with an automatic gun, a pistol, a bayonet, a baton, knife, and one or more hand grenades. The accused, in his position as a commander at the camp, had responsibility to ensure the proper treatment of the detainees. Rather than doing so, the accused chose to actively and brutally mistreat detainees by his own criminal acts, which thereby formed a form of encouragement to those under and alongside of him to do the same. Those fortunate enough to leave Susica camp alive in 1992 were not resettled back to the homes in which they left as many of those homes were destroyed, looted, or occupied by Serb residents. More importantly, they were not welcome into the municipality of which they once formed an essential part. It was never the case that Susica camp was a safe haven for those non-Serbs that would have otherwise been in danger in surrounding villages; there was simply no safe place for them, neither in or outside of the camp. Women, children, and elderly detainees were expelled to Bosnian-Muslim-held territory around Kladanj and Cerska. Military-aged men and some women were transferred to other places of detention in Bosnia, respectively Batkovic camp in Bijeljina municipality and Pelemis, a village in Serb-held territory in Kladanj municipality. Following the killing of the last group of 100 or more detainees at a site near Susica camp called Debelo Brdo, the camp was disbanded, having fulfilled its role in eliminating the Muslim and other non-Serb population from Vlasenica municipality. Your Honours, I would now like to show a short video clip of Susica camp, if you think it will be of assistance to you, with the witness's testimony. As I said previously, the next witness has very poor vision, so she can't refer to any visual aids. But I'm in Your Honours' hands in relation to the length of time, whether you'd like to see that short five-minute video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Of course it's for -- as the Prosecution to present its case, however, we should take care that the witnesses have the necessary time to give their testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, on this video, you'll see now - it's just being called up now - you'll see the front of Susica camp, looking towards the hangar in which they were detained. It should be coming up in one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That's the front of the hangar. And now we're looking back towards Vlasenica. And that pole there is the A-pole where a number of people were beaten, especially a number of the victims in the counts in the indictment. This is view looking at the back of the Susica camp away from Vlasenica town, bearing in mind that Vlasenica was about one-and-a-half kilometres away. This is outside of the camp. That's the warehouse that was right next to the one which the detainees -- sorry, that's looking towards Vlasenica -- Here is the hangar. This is where the detainees were kept. And this is back of the hangar. It's full of military equipment now, but at that time the hangar was completely empty. This video was taken in 1996 by Tribunal investigators. The corner that you're looking at now is the back corner of the hangar, and this is what witnesses may refer to as the punishment corner, where a number of the victims in the indictment subsequently died after being beaten. That's not the front door, that's a side rear door and that wasn't used as an entry or exit point at the camp in 1992. It was generally locked. And now the camera is panning towards the front of the hangar from the back. Again, those chairs, et cetera, weren't in the hangar when the detainees were kept there. It was completely empty. The hangar is quite large. As I stated earlier, it could fit about 4 to 5 hundred people in it. This is the side wall of the hangar, going up towards the entrance to the hangar. There's largely one entrance to the hangar that was used. Obviously the truck wasn't there at the time. That's the front door of the hangar. There's a small door and two very large double doors. Again, this is the sole place where the detainees were kept during their detention at the camp. This is looking out towards -- now we're look out towards the A-pole, which are those two wooden posts which can be seen there, which is what the detainees would have seen if they were trying to look at the beatings that were occurring outside of the hangar. The hangar is, as I said, about 35 metres by 13 metres. We'll now cut to some footage of the guardhouse. This -- there's the A-pole again. That's the entrance to the compound. That's where people were brought in and were taken out. It's looking at the front door of the hangar again and panning back. There's the A-pole in view. I think it's about 17 metres from the front door of the hangar and about 20 metres or so from the guardhouse. We're now looking into the front door of the guardhouse, which is about 15 metres away from the camp. There's two rooms in it. That room faces away from the hangar. And this room here which we walk into now, that window directly faces onto the front of the hangar, and that's about 11 metres. This is where the guards stayed, and this is where the accused slept often at the camp. Although the lighting is dark, it's just panning around this room where the accused slept, and this is where detainees were brought in and interrogated. That's a bed in the room. It's very difficult to see. Again, this was taken in 1996, so the set-up, we can't guarantee that it was exactly the same as in 1992. There's a side window looking towards the hangar there, and here is a front window that looked towards the entrance of the camp and also the front of the camp. And that's coming out of the room now. There's just a small hallway between the two rooms. Now, this is the second room, the second room that's away from the hangar. And this was a room where there appeared to be some kitchen facilities. That's the end of the video, Your Honours. Now I'd like to call the first witness. Or would Your Honours like a short break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No. Let's start immediately. And may I ask the usher please to escort the first witness into the courtroom. What is the estimated time you would need for the first witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I think, Your Honours, we had planned about 30 to 40 minutes for each witness, and then that would allow Your Honours 15 or 20 minutes for questioning. If Your Honours would like the testimony to be shorter, as far as Prosecution witnesses are concerned, we're happy to oblige as well. We'll be dictated by Your Honours' views.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We are limited until 1.30 today, and so we have to make for technical reasons the next break at 10.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I'll take that into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So if you could take this into account and maybe the questions are limited. But let's see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So once again, to be on the safe side, no pseudonym needed; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No pseudonym?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: No pseudonym. No protective measures, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Madam Habiba Hadzic, a very good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind and give us your solemn declaration. I intend to read it, and if you'd please be so kind, repeat it. Rule 90 of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence provide that the solemn declaration reads as follows: "I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth." Would you please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I answer? I can speak. I have a sore throat, but I still can speak. I will speak the truth and only the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And you solemnly declare to do so; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Should you have any problems, please tell the Bench immediately that we can take the necessary measures. The Prosecution will now start questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Just to be clear, the witness statements of this witness have been tendered into evidence. Do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps with the indulgence of the Court and my learned friends, what I would like to do in relation to this examination, because of the shortness of time, lead the witness in a number of areas, apart from a couple of key issues. And I hope my friend understands the reason for that approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Hadzic. Can you please tell us your name, how old you are, and what ethnicity you are.

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: My name is Habiba Hadzic. I was born on the 15th of March, 1943, and I'm a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions about what happened to you at Susica camp, what you saw, and what you -- how it made you feel then and now. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And Ms. Hadzic, you have very poor eyesight, and it makes it difficult for you to read and see small detail; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can't see well enough to read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, just to interrupt, to clarify. On the transcript, it reads that your birthday is the 15th of March; whereas, in your statement it reads 5 March, 1943.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. You may continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And on Saturday, Ms. Hadzic, we met. And one of your statements was read out to you, a statement taken by a Tribunal investigator in 1994 and 1996. Do you remember that statement being read out to you?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was there anything in that statement that you couldn't remember or you felt was incorrect as to what you experienced at Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: All that I said, that I stated, is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: From your statement, Ms. Hadzic, you were at Susica camp for about two months; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps a bit longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you first arrived at the camp, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: To the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were any other members of your family taken to the hangar as well?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: First the children were taken there, then me, my sister-in-law, her husband, and her two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court what your two children's names are.

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Enis Hadzic, and Bernis Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how old were they?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Enis was born on the 18th of September, 1961; and Bernis Hadzic was born on the 4th of April, 1963.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What did you see when you got into the hangar when you first arrived at the camp? Who was in there?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: There were a lot of people, and women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was the camp full or empty or half full? Can you describe?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: It was jam-packed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you left the camp some two months later, was the camp still jam-packed, or were there less people in there?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, sometimes there were fewer, sometimes more. Most of the time there were a lot of people inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Whilst you were in the hangar and you were staying at the camp, were you allowed to move freely outside of the hangar in the compound area?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: No. Only when Jenki would order so, only when he would tell us what to do. Those were the only times we were able to move around.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court who Jenki is.

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what's his first name?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: I can't remember now. I know that he's Nikolic, also known as Jenki.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that he -- you said that he would -- only he would allow -- excuse me. You said that you were only allowed to move freely outside of the hangar when Jenki would allow. Who was -- who was in charge at the camp?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'm asking you who was in charge at the camp.

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: He was, Jenki. He was in command. Nikolic, also known as Jenki.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you mention in your same another person that had some command responsibility at the camp, and his name was Veljko Basic. Did he also --

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Basic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did he also have some command at the camp, some control?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, he would come in the morning, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who was at the camp more often? Was it Jenki or was it Veljko Basic?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Jenki.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who guarded the people at the camp? How many -- how many people were making sure that yourself and the others were not leaving the hangar?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, sometimes there would be ten of them or eight, twelve, depending on how they are assigned by Jenki.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So you've mentioned that Veljko Basic had some -- a command at the camp and Jenki had some command at the camp. Was there anyone else in the guards -- was there anyone else in the guards that showed some command or authority over other guards, other than Jenki and Veljko Basic?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: No. Jenki held everything under his control and issued orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How often was Jenki at the camp? Was he there every day or every second day or once a week?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Every day, for most of the time, both in the evenings and in the afternoons. He was there most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know where Jenki slept at night?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Sometimes when we wanted to fetch water, there was this guardhouse where his bed was, where he slept. It was a small guardhouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said --

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: That's where he was accommodated, where he spent his time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How often did he stay at -- stay at the camp? How often did he sleep there? Was it weekly, or was it more than that?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't know everything. I would see him often coming back, coming around midnight. I would see him when he would come up to the hangar. But otherwise, we were closed in in the hangar, and I couldn't see whether he had gone somewhere to spend the night or he was still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that the bed in the guardhouse was his bed. Did -- did anyone else use the bed?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, sometimes maybe another guard would use it, but for the most part it was Jenki.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did Veljko Basic ever sleep at the camp?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Not that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Where did you sleep in the camp?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: I slept between my two children in the hangar. And when Jenki would give us orders to that effect, we would even go outside the camp to the houses nearby. Sometimes I would sleep in a lorry, together with one of my children.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that you stayed at the camp for about two months and that sometimes you slept outside of the camp. About how many nights did you sleep outside of the camp?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, every time Jenki would order us, we spent the night in one of those nearby houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that when Jenki ordered that you sleep outside of the camp. Did any other guards or Veljko Basic order you to sleep outside of the camp?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you slept in the camp, what did you sleep on? Were there any mattresses or anything to make your sleep comfortable?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: No. No. For the most part, we slept on bare concrete or wooden boards. But when he would be angry, he wouldn't even allow us to lie on those wooden boards. They would be taken out. They would be removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you have much space to sleep in? Could you stretch out without touching other detainees?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Sometimes yes; sometimes not. Sometimes there were too many people and you had to squeeze. Sometimes you could even fall asleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How comfortable were you when you slept?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Awful.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How often did you eat at the camp? Did you eat three times a day, once a day?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Once a day. We got one meal a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court what you ate, what you were given to eat.

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, it was food that had gone bad. Sometimes we would be given tins that had turned bad and we would have trouble going to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you were at the camp, did you receive enough food or did you want more?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: We did, but we didn't get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who got it? If you didn't get it, who got it?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, people would sometimes bring us food, and Veljko Basic would not allow us to receive it. When Veljko Basic would go away, Jenki would issue orders that food be given to those to whom it was brought.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned in your statement that you saw the mistreatment of a number of detainees by the accused, and I'm referring to Mevludin Hatunic, Durmo Handzic.

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Muharem Kolarevic.

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Muharem Kolarevic, and a man from Papraca, Rasid, and the other one was Zekic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you explain why on the one hand the accused was involved in the beating of these men and at the other time was providing detainees with more food?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, he did not exactly provide more food. Jenki would take those men out and then would bring them back to the hangar when they had already been beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you left -- when you left the camp, had you lost weight?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were you able to wash your clothes at the camp?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: No. I asked for permission from time to time to go home, but very soon somebody would turn up and tell me, "Come on. Come on. Come back."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were you able to wash yourself at the camp, to make a shower or bathe?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were you provided any hygienic products like toothpaste or soap or deodorant so that you wouldn't smell?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: No. No, we were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned in your statement that many people were beaten at the camp by the accused and others; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In relation to the beatings generally by the accused or others, about how often was that occurring? Was it occurring once a week, daily, a couple of times a week? Can you give us a feeling of how often people were beaten at Susica camp.

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: During my stay there, at the Susica camp, Mevludin Hatunic, Durmo, were beaten up; both died. Asim Zildzic was beaten up and once when we were lined up to go to the toilets, I saw him carried on a stretcher. His eye was knocked out; I'm talking about Asim Zildzic. I often used to see Djidje being beaten by Jenki. He would spill water on the concrete and make him sit there, hungry, not giving him any food.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a person called Fikret Arnaut who was at the camp; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Which Fikret?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I think in your statement you referred to him --

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. His name is Fikret, and the other man's name is Fadil Huremovic. The two of them died; they were ill.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were they given any medical care, the two of those men that died? Did any doctors visit the camp, or were they taken to the hospital in town?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you tell us how Fadil Huremovic died. What did he die of?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, he was simply unable to stand up on his feet. His wife was abused and he was no longer able to suffer that. He just couldn't get up. He was bedridden.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, bearing in mind the shortness of time, I would like to spend another ten minutes with this witness. I don't know whether Your Honour wants to break now or to come back following the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's appropriate to have a break. May I ask all participants to understand that the break will be shorter than usual. We will resume ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you just to focus during the next ten minutes on the core issues of the testimony, and especially what is included in the indictment. Thank you. So you have the floor until 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, Ms. Hadzic, I mean, you mentioned that Fikret died at the camp. Is that Fikret Arnaut or is that someone else? In your statement, you mentioned a person called Cice, who has -- who had a nickname of Cice and his name was Fikret Arnaut. Is it the same person, or are you thinking of someone different?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: That is Kuljancic Fadil and Huremovic died. Whereas, Cice, succumbed to the beating in the camp. His name is Cice. That's how I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for Your Honours's information, Cice is Fikret Arnaut in the indictment. It's referred to there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that Cice succumbed to the beating at the camp. What do you mean by "succumbed"? Did he die at the camp, or was he still there when you left?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: He died while I was there, Cice did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you see who was doing the beating of Cice?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: I did not see. I only saw Jenki bring him onto the wet concrete floor. He sat there. But who beat him there is something I did not see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How often was Cice beaten even though you didn't see it? Did you see the effects of any beating on Cice whilst you were at the camp? And if so, how often did you see those signs?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: A few times; two, three times. He could not sit down, let alone stand up. That is how badly they would beat him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that you saw Jenki bring Cice onto the wet concrete floor. Where was Cice brought from? Was it -- are you saying from outside of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. From outside the hangar he brought him into the hangar, and he sat on that wet concrete floor, and he said, "You raped my mother," and then he cursed and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you ever try and help Cice, in relation to the beatings he received?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: He asked me to give him some cookies. I threw some cookies, but I did not see Jenki at the door. He walked up, and he crushed the biscuits with his boot, and he ordered me to go outside to the external toilet and he slapped me once, and I didn't do anything about it. The second time, he hit me with a rifle butt, and my arm is wounded because of that. I passed out and somebody tried to help me but Jenki kicked him and told him to go away. Then I came to by an old lady, who was 93 years old and who was telling me, "Things will get better. Things will get better." And he was shouting, "She did not die. She did not die. She's alive."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Why did Cice ask you for the biscuits -- the cookies? Why didn't he get them himself?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: They wouldn't let him have any. He was hungry and he asked me, "Could you give me one?" And I threw it across the floor, but he did not eat it. Jenki came and stomped on it. It was hard and it wasn't any good really, but he was hungry and he would have appreciated whatever he could have gotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that you did some work at the camp. Can you tell the Court what work you did inside the camp.

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: What Jenki ordered me to do. I would scrub his room, and then he would stretch his feet out so that I'd wash them and put cream on them, things like that. Then I'd wash the dishes when there was this one lunch. Well, at any rate, I had to do whatever he ordered me to do. I did not dare say no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were there any other guards ordering you to do any work at the camp?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: No. There was a blondish one, one of his -- there was something wrong with one of his eyes. He cursed at me. My daughter-in-law came and brought one of the children so that I could see them, and then he said, "Your daughter-in-law is good-looking." And then he cursed her. And then the -- when the guard cursed my daughter-in-law, then I said, "My son will curse your wife," and then Jenki walked up and said, "What was all of this about?" And I told him and he said, "You said the right thing."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that you had to wash the -- Jenki's feet. Was there a problem? Was there a medical problem with his feet?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: No. Just like that, by way of refreshment. That's what he wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how often did you have to do that?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I was not the only one. Sija Zepco was there, Nesiba, Saha Berbic, so I did not have to do everything on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, these people that you've just mentioned, are they women that had to do work at the camp as well?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned Sija and Nesiba and Saha. When you left the camp, were they still there? At the end?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Have you ever seen them again or do you know of them having been alive --

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: -- in the camp?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard - I did not see - that they were sent to Pelemis and killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say "Pelemis," do you know what was at Pelemis?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You've explained -- or perhaps -- sorry, I'll ask another question. You mentioned that you received an injury from Jenki. You said he hit your arm with a rifle butt and it caused you some pain. Has that pain gone away?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: No. I shall remain disabled, as far as this arm is concerned. If necessary, I can show it to you. I'm supposed to have it x-rayed right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: No, there's no need to show it to us. But can you explain, tell us which elbow it is, is it the left or right, and basically explain the injury.

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: The right one. The right elbow, the one here. It's as if there were a hole in it. It hurts me. I can't take a bath on my own. Let me put it this way: It hurts really bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Other than the injury to the arm, were there any other conditions -- health conditions that developed after you left Susica camp that you believe are related to your stay at the camp and the conditions that you suffered?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Afterwards, when I left, I had a bit of high blood-sugar level but then it got much higher, so I really had this problem. I also have some heart trouble, that angina thing, and I have all my findings that can prove that. Now that my children are no longer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you say that your children are no longer there, when you left the camp on the last time, was your son Enis and Bernis still at the camp?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And have you seen either of your sons ever again?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: No. No. When I was sent as a messenger to Cerska, 14 of us messengers came bearing the same message. I was running there to see where my children were, what they were doing, how they were, things like that, but I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you believe that your sons are alive today? If they are alive, would they have contacted you?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: No, they are not alive. Jenki knows that. I just wish he knew in which mass grave they were so that their mother could give them a dignified funeral, so that their mother would know where they are buried. But I don't know. I've never found out. They took away their personal IDs. They have nothing in order to prove who they were. He's the only one who knows, and I would like to ask him if he knows to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mrs. Hadzic, if I can ask you a couple questions first: You were at the camp -- I know this is very upsetting for you.

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: What can I do about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can just take two minutes to finish the last two questions with the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were at the camp for about two months. You mentioned that the sleeping conditions were terrible, you couldn't wash, you couldn't shower, you couldn't keep clean, the food was terrible, you were forced -- you were forced to --

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I can just finish the question; you were beaten, you saw the beatings of other people. How did it feel staying in the camp night after Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 241 to 245. night --

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: What I would see was less. I mean, he would take people out and bring them back beaten up and then Koljevic, Zekic from Popica [phoen] and then Mujkic, he would take them out. I did know see who they were, but I heard three gunshots and the hangar was closed. And the morning, when they lined us up at the toilet, men on one side, women on this side, and then Muharem - I know him, because he's my friend's brother, and his son was there too - and then my children were whispering to me, "Mama, there's Muharem." There was a small TAM truck and they were lying dead on that truck. Now, where they drove their bodies to, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Mrs. Hadzic, I've just got two last questions for you. So if you could listen to them. I know it's difficult. What was the feeling like in the hangar? What was the atmosphere like, bearing in mind all the conditions you suffered and the other detainees suffered and the beatings that were occurring? What was the atmosphere? What did it feel like to stay in that camp at night and during the day?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: What did it feel like? The stench was the worst possible, and you had to suffer it. In the morning and in the evening, people went to the toilet. There were buckets there by the door. People would have to go. The food was bad. It went foul. It was terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And I'd like to ask you: What is it like today? It's about 11 years or so since you were at the camp and you went through a lot of experiences there and you saw a lot. Has it affected you psychologically today, or do you feel fit and well and able to get on with your life and not think about Susica camp? Does it affect you at all today?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: How it affects me? There are two wounds that are there: Sadness, pain, everything I went through in the camp. My children were innocent and they lost their lives. They were killed. I could not even remember his proper name a few minutes ago. Dragan Nikolic, nicknamed Jenki. He killed them just because they were Muslims. That is what I have to say. I can't say anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And one last question: Is there anything that you'd like to say to the Judges about the impact that your stay at Susica camp has had on you? If not, that's --

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Everything. If I were to tell you everything, what could I tell you? I am a sick woman now. I have high blood sugar. I have a weak heart. It is so bad. My feet went numb while I've been sitting here. I have nothing to hope for. This mother cannot take it much longer. You will see. I will die of sadness and sorrow. My husband is also sick and he cries often. He hides from me when he cries, but then I follow him and then we cry. What can we do? I would just like to ask Dragan to tell me where they are, in which mass grave, so that their mother could give them a dignified funeral. I want to give them a proper burial, and then I can go away myself. That is what I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Hadzic. Thank you very much for coming today. I know it's been very difficult for you. But we appreciate your efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness is plainly in a very distressed state at the moment. I don't want to add to that distress, but I am conscious of the passage of time. But it may be better that she's allowed to recover her composure before I ask her any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's appropriate to have a break of about five minutes, and this would also allow you to contact your client, whether or not he wants to answer the question the witness put to him. Thank you. The trial stays adjourned for five minutes. --- Break taken at 11.10 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Morrison, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Madam, I just want to ask you a few questions related to a number of incidents in the camp and to get your reaction to a number of names that I'm going to put to you. And please forgive me if my pronunciation is not exact. Do you recall a man called Kraljevic, Mico?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Mico Kraljevic. Yes, I do. He had his own specials from Rogosija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: He's a person that would occasionally come to the camp whilst you were there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: And indeed, you understood from Dragan Nikolic himself that this man was Dragan Nikolic's superior, his commander?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: They cooperated. Often they would roast a lamb or two. Kraljevic would come. He would stay there with his specials. The music would be blaring. They'd corral us in that hangar. That's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: But to answer my question, and I'm simply repeating something from your statement, that Dragan Nikolic said to you that he had to do what Mico said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just for the record, may I ask Defence counsel to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they cooperated, Mico and Dragan. Nevertheless, Dragan had the main say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: For Your Honours's reference, it's on page 3, on the third paragraph from the -- the full reference number ends with the last four digits 1494 on the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. The first statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: You've also mentioned somebody called Basic or -- is that correct? Veljko Basic?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, Veljko Basic. Before he was a policeman and while I was up there, he was warden of the camp. When Dragan ordered me to wash the dishes, Veljko was sitting there where Dragan would usually rest, and he pretended to bring a doctor to examine the civilians. And there was a car there in front of the fountain, and Elvis sat there, Raco, who had lost a brother in Cerska. And then Veljko asked me whether I had seen who had taken this man away. When Pejac took Nazif, "Sikara" out, behind that third building he hit him once and he said, "Ah." And then the second time, "Ah." And the third time, in the manger. And then they drove them off. Veljko asked me whether I saw this. I did see it, but I didn't dare say so. He would have beaten me until nightfall. And I said, "No. See, Dragan is forcing me to wash the dishes. Why didn't you tell me to watch?" And he said, "Well, his wife asked me or called me and asked me where Nazif was." Well, that's what Zeljko said to me later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: So you've said already in testimony to this Trial Chamber that Veljko Basic on occasion stopped Jenki from giving food that had been brought for the prisoners. Is that food that was brought to the camp from relatives of the detainees?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Veljko would not allow it. He chased them away. I'm telling the truth. Jenki would say, "Wait for him to leave and then take this food." What is true is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: And once Basic had left the camp, Jenki could allow that food to be given to the prisoners, would he not?

utterances.speaker: HABIBA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
